overview:
What historians now bundle under a single name was in fact a long series of campaigns, truces and collapses between the kings of England and France, running from 1337 to 1453 with decades of quiet in between. The immediate trigger was Gascony: Philip VI declared the English king's duchy of Aquitaine confiscated in 1337, and Edward III — a grandson of Philip IV through his mother, passed over for the French crown in 1328 — responded by styling himself the rightful king of France. Behind the dynastic claim lay harder interests: the Gascon wine trade, the Flemish cloth towns that bought English wool, and the awkwardness of an English king holding French land as a vassal. Fighting spread well beyond the two kingdoms, drawing in Scotland, Castile, Portugal, the Low Countries and above all the dukes of Burgundy, whose choice of side repeatedly decided the war's direction.

The first phase belonged to England. A naval victory at Sluys in 1340 secured the Channel; Crécy in 1346 and Poitiers in 1356 — the latter ending with the French king a prisoner — showed what dismounted men-at-arms and massed longbowmen could do to mounted chivalry, and Calais fell after a year's siege in 1347. Between the set-piece battles ran the chevauchée, the deliberate burning of crops and villages to humiliate a king who could not protect his people. The Treaty of Brétigny in 1360 gave Edward an enlarged Aquitaine in exchange for renouncing the French throne, but the settlement did not hold. Charles V and his constable Bertrand du Guesclin clawed back most of the losses from 1369 by avoiding battle altogether, and a Castilian fleet destroyed English shipping off La Rochelle in 1372. The war then guttered out into truce until Henry V reopened it in 1415, won Agincourt against long odds, and by the Treaty of Troyes in 1420 had himself recognised as heir to the mad Charles VI. His death in 1422 left an infant to inherit that claim. The turn came in 1429, when a peasant girl from Lorraine, Joan of Arc, helped break the siege of Orléans and saw Charles VII crowned at Reims; she was captured, tried by a pro-English court at Rouen and burned in 1431, and her conviction was annulled in 1456. Burgundy's defection to Charles VII in 1435 was decisive in a way no battle was. Formigny in 1450 cost England Normandy, and at Castillon in 1453 the entrenched guns of Jean Bureau destroyed John Talbot's army and with it English Gascony. No treaty ended the war; the fighting simply stopped, and Calais remained English until 1558.
significance: The war outlasted the world that began it. It broke the primacy of the armoured horseman, first through the longbow and the disciplined infantry line, then through the siege and field artillery that made Castillon a preview of gunpowder warfare; and it forced both crowns to build the machinery that pays for long wars — permanent taxation, standing companies, war finance and, in England, a Parliament that grew powerful by granting the money. France emerged territorially whole and its monarchy strengthened, with a national story it would tell about itself for centuries, Joan of Arc at its centre. England, bankrupt and stripped of a continental inheritance held since Henry II, turned inward into the dynastic bloodletting of the Wars of the Roses and, over the following century, toward the sea. For the people of northern and western France, the lasting legacy was less glorious: generations of raiding, plague and unpaid soldiers turned brigand.
coverage: Written from general reference accounts of the war's causes, phases and outcome, checked against a detailed account of Castillon; the dataset's ninety events are heavily weighted toward pitched battles and sieges, which is exactly the distortion the sources warn against, since most of the war was raiding, garrison duty and truce rather than battle. Thin here and in the record generally: the experience of civilians and common soldiers, reliable casualty and army-size figures (chronicle numbers are inflated and contested), the Breton, Castilian and Burgundian theatres, and the war's economic history. The name itself is a nineteenth-century French coinage, and the 1337 and 1453 endpoints are a later tidy-up rather than dates anyone alive then would have recognised.
